chapters.title: Solar energy, Earth movements and geographical time
objectives: Distinguish rotation from revolution and explain their effects.
Use latitude, longitude and time differences with stated assumptions.
Explain seasonal changes without confusing distance and tilt.
paragraphs: The Sun supplies most of the energy that drives surface weather and plant growth. Earth is the third planet from the Sun, orbiting between Venus and Mars. Gravity keeps planets in orbit while their existing motion carries them forward. The solar system formed from a rotating cloud of gas and dust; scientific explanations draw on observations and physical evidence rather than direct observation of its formation.

Rotation is Earth’s turning on its axis, taking approximately 24 hours relative to the Sun. A place faces daylight while turned towards the Sun and night while turned away. Because rotation is eastward, the Sun appears to move westward across the sky. A moving shadow can therefore provide evidence of apparent solar movement, but its exact direction depends on place and season.

Revolution is Earth’s movement around the Sun in about 365¼ days. Earth’s axis is tilted about 23½ degrees relative to a line perpendicular to the orbital plane. As Earth revolves, the hemisphere tilted towards the Sun generally receives higher solar angles and longer days. Seasons follow this changing angle and duration, not simply the varying Earth–Sun distance. Near the Equator, rainfall seasons can be more noticeable than temperature seasons.

Latitude measures angular distance north or south of the Equator; longitude measures angular distance east or west of the prime meridian. Parallels are circles of latitude; meridians meet at the poles. Earth turns through 360 degrees in 24 hours, giving 15 degrees per hour or four minutes per degree. Longitude calculations give local solar time differences; actual civil time follows agreed time zones and may differ.
examples: Local solar time at 30°E is 12:00. A place at 45°E lies 15° farther east: 15 ÷ 15 = 1 hour ahead, so its local solar time is 13:00. This is a solar-time model, not a claim about legal time zones.
At 20°W it is 09:20 local solar time. At 10°E the difference is 30°: 30 × 4 = 120 minutes. Move east and add two hours: 11:20.

In a classroom model, hold a tilted globe with its axis pointing in the same direction while moving it around a lamp. The hemisphere tilted towards the lamp receives more direct light and longer exposure. Rotating the globe explains day and night; carrying it around the lamp explains the annual pattern.

chapters.title: Comparing landforms, drainage and inland waters
objectives: Recognise major relief forms using height and shape.
Explain drainage links between land and water bodies.
Use comparative geographical evidence.
paragraphs: Relief describes differences in surface elevation and land shape. A mountain rises prominently above its surroundings, a plateau is an extensive elevated surface with relatively level parts, and a plain has gentle relief. Height alone does not decide the name: a high plateau can contain mountains and valleys. Describe both elevation and local shape before assigning a label to a landscape.

A river flows down a gradient through a channel. Tributaries join a main stream; the land drained by the connected streams forms a drainage basin. A watershed is the higher boundary separating neighbouring basins. Water on opposite sides of a divide can enter different rivers. Weathering, erosion, transport and deposition change a basin over time, while vegetation and settlement affect runoff.

Lakes occupy inland depressions filled with water. Some have river outlets; others lose much of their water through evaporation and seepage. A lake without an outlet may accumulate dissolved salts, but the actual salinity depends on its water and mineral balance. Wetlands have water at or near the surface for significant periods and can store floodwater, support habitats and filter some pollutants.

Continents are major land masses and oceans are connected bodies of salt water. Africa contains varied relief and important inland waters, including Lakes Victoria, Tanganyika and Nyasa/Malawi. A location description should combine a named feature, its position and a relevant characteristic. Claims about flooding or water use need evidence such as river levels, rainfall records, field observations and mapped settlement, because one photograph cannot describe every season.
examples: Site A: elevation 1,500 m, broad rolling surface; Site B: summit 1,450 m, steep sides rising 700 m above nearby land. A may be a plateau and B a mountain: relative relief and shape matter alongside absolute elevation.

A basin receives 100 units of rain. If 35 evaporate, 20 infiltrate into storage and 45 run off, the simplified balance is 100 = 35 + 20 + 45. Real basins also have changing stores and flows across boundaries.

River U joins River V before V enters a lake. U is a tributary, the meeting point is a confluence, and their combined catchment belongs to the drainage basin. A ridge between them and River W can form a watershed.

chapters.title: Vegetation zones, adaptation and field evidence
objectives: Compare forest, savanna and arid vegetation.
Connect plant adaptations to environmental conditions.
Collect vegetation evidence responsibly.
paragraphs: Natural vegetation is plant cover developing under local environmental conditions, although human activity modifies most inhabited landscapes. Vegetation zones describe broad patterns, not sharp boundaries. Temperature, rainfall amount and seasonality, soil, altitude, drainage, fire and grazing interact. Two places with similar annual rainfall may support different plants if one has a much longer dry season or poorly drained soil.

Humid tropical forest commonly has many broad-leaved trees and a layered canopy where moisture and warmth support growth. Dense upper foliage reduces light reaching the forest floor, favouring shade-tolerant plants. Savanna commonly combines grasses with scattered trees or shrubs and has a marked wet and dry season. Tree spacing varies with soils, water, fire and land use, so a single tree does not identify an entire vegetation zone.

Arid and semi-arid vegetation is often sparse and includes plants with features that reduce water loss or improve water access. Small leaves or thorns reduce exposed leaf area, thick cuticles limit water loss, succulent tissues store water and some roots spread widely or reach deeply. No single adaptation belongs to every dryland plant. Highland vegetation can change with altitude because temperature and moisture conditions change.

Vegetation investigation should link a claim to a measured observation. Use a small quadrat or a line transect, record the same categories at each site and note soil moisture, shade and signs of disturbance. Avoid damaging plants or entering unsafe areas. A table showing several samples is stronger than a selected photograph, but a small school survey cannot justify a claim about an entire region. Distinguish observed plant cover from your explanation of why it occurs.
examples: Five equal quadrats have grass cover 40%, 50%, 60%, 30% and 70%. Mean cover = 250 ÷ 5 = 50%. The range is 70 − 30 = 40 percentage points, showing considerable local variation.

On a transect, shaded sites have fewer grasses and deeper leaf litter. A reasonable explanation is reduced light beneath trees. Soil moisture and trampling may also differ; measure these before attributing everything to shade.
A shrub has tiny leaves and a thick waxy surface. These features can reduce water loss. They support an adaptation hypothesis, but identifying its species or exact climate requires further evidence.

chapters.title: Topographic maps: contours, slopes and route decisions
objectives: Read contour heights and slope patterns.
Calculate gradient and construct a simple profile.
Justify route choices with map evidence.
paragraphs: A topographic map represents surface features with symbols, scale and relief information. Begin with the title, key, north arrow and scale, then read the contour interval before interpreting heights. A contour joins points at equal elevation above a reference level. Adjacent contours usually differ by a constant vertical interval; the space between them on paper shows horizontal distance, not another height measurement.

Closely spaced contours indicate a steep slope because a given height change occurs over a short horizontal distance. Widely spaced contours indicate gentler slopes. Concentric closed contours with increasing values inward commonly represent a hill. A valley usually makes contours bend upstream into a V; confirm the direction using height values and any river symbol. A closed contour alone does not prove a hill if heights or depression markings indicate otherwise.

Gradient compares vertical rise with horizontal distance measured in the same units. A 40 m rise over 800 m gives 40:800 = 1:20. This is different from the slope distance actually walked. To draw a profile, place a paper strip along a line, mark contour crossings and heights, transfer their horizontal positions to graph paper, then plot and connect heights. A steep-looking profile may result from vertical exaggeration, so label both scales.

Route selection combines relief with other mapped evidence. A short straight route can cross a steep slope, river or wet ground; a longer route may be safer or easier to build. A map cannot establish current bridge condition, path access or seasonal flooding by itself. Explain a proposed route by citing the contour spacing, crossings and distance, then identify what must be checked on the ground.
examples: Contours labelled 100, 120, 140 and 160 m have a 20 m interval. A point exactly on the 140 m line is 140 m high. A point between 140 and 160 m is within that interval; do not report an exact height without further evidence.
A route rises from 200 to 260 m across 1.5 km horizontally. Rise = 60 m; run = 1,500 m; gradient = 60:1,500 = 1:25. Every 25 m horizontally corresponds to an average 1 m rise.

Profile table: distance from A (m): 0 | 100 | 200 | 300 | 400; height (m): 100 | 120 | 160 | 180 | 180. The steepest sampled section is 100–200 m, rising 40 m in 100 m. The final segment is level in this simplified sample.

chapters.title: Statistical maps, rates and honest comparisons
objectives: Choose maps suitable for counts, rates and movement.
Interpret a data table alongside a statistical map.
Recognise misleading map comparisons.
paragraphs: Statistical maps show the spatial distribution of numerical information. A choropleth map shades defined areas according to a value or class; a dot map uses repeated dots to represent quantities; proportional symbols vary symbol size with quantity. Flow maps show movement using lines or arrows whose widths may represent volume. Every map needs a title, time period, key and source so readers know what is being compared.

For a choropleth map, a rate or density is often more useful than a raw total when areas differ in population or size. Population density equals population divided by land area. The average describes the whole mapped area and does not show each settlement. Shading an entire district with one class must not be interpreted as proof that every part has the same density.

Class intervals change the map’s visual pattern. Non-overlapping classes such as 0–49, 50–99 and 100–149 people per km² place each integer value in one class. Equal intervals are easy to compare, while other classifications may emphasise different patterns. A dot represents a stated quantity and an approximate distribution; it does not automatically identify a real household at the exact dot position.

Read the table before explaining the map. Check units, dates, missing values and whether geographical boundaries match. Correlation between two mapped variables can suggest a question but does not establish cause. A district with many shops might also have a large population; shops per thousand residents can answer a different question from total shops. Use both absolute totals and suitable rates when the decision requires them.
examples: Teaching table: Area A: 12,000 people, 200 km², 24 shops; B: 9,000 people, 50 km², 27 shops; C: 20,000 people, 400 km², 20 shops. Densities are 60, 180 and 50 people/km² respectively. C has the largest population, while B has the greatest density.
Using the same table, shops per 1,000 people are A: 24/12,000 × 1,000 = 2; B: 3; C: 1. A total-shop map and a shop-rate map answer different questions.
If one dot represents 500 people, A needs 12,000 ÷ 500 = 24 dots. An exactly divisible teaching total is convenient; real data may require rounding that must be stated in the legend.

chapters.title: Earth-system connections and photographic field investigation
objectives: Trace exchanges among Earth systems.
Use photographs as evidence with explicit limits.
Plan a safe repeatable field investigation.
paragraphs: The crust is Earth’s thin outer rocky layer, generally about 5–70 km thick; oceanic crust is usually thinner than continental crust. The mantle extends down to roughly 2,900 km and is mainly solid rock that can flow very slowly over geological time. The core contains an outer liquid part and an inner solid part, composed largely of iron with other elements. Increasing pressure helps explain why the inner core remains solid despite high temperature.

The atmosphere contains gases surrounding Earth, the hydrosphere includes water in liquid, solid and gaseous forms, and the biosphere includes living organisms and their zones of life. These systems overlap rather than forming completely separate boxes. Soil contains minerals, water, air and organisms. A tree takes water from soil, exchanges gases with air and returns moisture through transpiration, connecting several systems.

A photograph records visible features from one position at one moment. Ground photographs can be divided into foreground, middle ground and background; oblique photographs look down at an angle, while vertical aerial photographs look approximately straight down. A title, date, location and viewing direction improve interpretation. Relative position in a photograph does not provide a uniform distance scale because perspective makes distant objects appear smaller.

Interpretation begins with observations: bare soil, tree cover, channel shape or visible buildings. Then propose explanations and identify evidence needed to test them. Muddy stream water after rain may be consistent with erosion, but a photograph cannot measure sediment concentration or prove its source. Repeat photographs from a fixed safe point, combine them with rainfall and stream observations, and protect people’s privacy. Never enter fast water or unstable slopes to obtain evidence.
examples: Rain falls on a wooded slope: atmosphere to hydrosphere; some water infiltrates soil; roots absorb it; plants transpire moisture into air. Clearing trees may alter these flows, but the size of the change depends on soil, slope and land management.

Photo log table: image P1 | 10:00 | fixed bridge viewpoint | after rain | brown stream, bare bank. P2 | 10:00 two dry days later | same viewpoint | clearer stream. The pair shows visible change; measured turbidity and upstream observations would test the proposed sediment explanation.

A ground image shows a large tree in the foreground and small buildings behind. The image alone cannot establish that the tree is taller than the buildings: different distances affect apparent size. Use known dimensions or a measured map for reliable comparisons.

chapters.title: Entrepreneurship theories: innovation, opportunity and uncertainty
objectives: Compare explanations of entrepreneurial action.
Apply theories to a local business scenario.
Distinguish evidence from entrepreneurial assumptions.
paragraphs: An entrepreneur organises resources to pursue an opportunity and accepts uncertainty about the result. Entrepreneurship is a process of identifying needs, developing an offer, arranging resources and learning from customers. Owning a business does not guarantee innovation or profit. A useful explanation identifies what a person does and why it creates value, rather than relying on a list of personality traits.

An innovation explanation emphasises new combinations: a new product, improved process, new market or different way of organising work. Innovation need not be a completely new invention. A food seller who introduces pre-orders to reduce waiting and waste changes the service process. The change becomes commercially useful only if customers value it and its benefits justify its costs.

An opportunity or alertness explanation emphasises noticing an unmet need, an overlooked resource or a mismatch between supply and demand. A learner may notice that nearby workers cannot buy affordable lunch during a short break. This observation suggests an opportunity, but demand must be tested. Interviews, small trials and observation of existing sellers provide stronger evidence than simply assuming every worker will buy.

An uncertainty explanation emphasises decisions whose outcomes cannot be known fully in advance. A trader may estimate demand but cannot know the exact number of buyers next month. Calculated risk involves gathering information, limiting potential loss and preparing alternatives; it does not mean ignoring danger. These explanations complement one another: one enterprise can notice a need, innovate in delivery and manage uncertainty at the same time.
examples: A tailor introduces appointments by message and groups similar jobs. Innovation lies in the scheduling process; evidence of value would include reduced waiting, fewer missed deadlines and repeat orders. A new label alone would not demonstrate improved value.

A fruit seller observes unsold ripe fruit and interviews ten nearby workers. Six express interest in small fruit portions. A limited paid trial tests actual purchases; six interested interviewees do not prove that six people will buy every day.

Two production choices have different possible losses: making 100 units may leave 40 unsold, while a 20-unit trial limits initial exposure. The smaller trial sacrifices some potential sales but provides information before expansion.

chapters.title: Enterprise skills: customer research, communication and negotiation
objectives: Collect usable customer evidence.
Communicate an offer clearly and ethically.
Negotiate while checking costs and promises.
paragraphs: Enterprise skills are learned abilities used to turn an idea into dependable action. Communication, numeracy, planning, problem-solving and teamwork support one another. A seller who understands customer needs but cannot calculate costs may price badly; a skilled producer who misses deadlines may lose trust. Skills improve through practice, feedback and records rather than through confidence alone.

Customer research begins with a focused decision, such as choosing package size or delivery time. Ask neutral questions about existing behaviour: what people currently buy, how often, at what price and what problems occur. A leading question such as “Would you buy our excellent cheap product?” encourages favourable answers. Include people beyond friends and record refusals or negative responses, because selective evidence creates false confidence.

A clear offer states what is supplied, the quantity or quality, price, delivery timing and any conditions. Listening matters as much as speaking: repeat the customer’s requirement and check ambiguities before accepting an order. Keep a simple order record with agreed details. Protect customer contact information, avoid false claims and do not promise delivery that the available materials or time cannot support.

Negotiation seeks an agreement acceptable to both sides. Prepare by estimating costs, deciding a minimum acceptable outcome and considering alternatives. A lower unit price may be workable for a large order if production savings cover the discount, but extra packaging or transport can erase the benefit. Confirm the final quantity, total charge, deadline and payment arrangement in a clear record; disagreement often follows assumptions that were never checked.
examples: Neutral survey question: “How many notebooks did you buy last month, and what size?” This gathers behaviour. “You want our better notebooks, don’t you?” is leading and gives weak evidence.

An order is 12 bags at 2,500 currency units each. Total = 12 × 2,500 = 30,000. Record bag size, collection date and whether payment is due at collection; the price calculation alone does not define the full agreement.

Unit cost is 1,600 and usual price is 2,000. A buyer requests 1,700 for 20 units. Contribution before other fixed costs is (1,700 − 1,600) × 20 = 2,000. An extra delivery cost of 2,500 would make that offer unattractive on these assumptions.

chapters.title: Sole-trader launch: feasibility, liability and a first-month plan
objectives: Assess whether a small sole-trader idea is feasible.
Explain ownership, control and personal exposure.
Prepare a practical launch plan and review criteria.
paragraphs: A sole proprietorship has one owner who makes decisions and receives the business’s profit or bears its loss. The owner can employ other people; one owner does not mean one worker. Direct control and simple decision-making can help a small business respond quickly, while limited finance, workload and dependence on the owner can restrict growth. The business may struggle if the owner becomes unavailable.

Unlimited liability means the owner may be personally responsible for business debts; business losses are not automatically limited to the amount initially invested. Keep business and personal records separate to understand performance, even where ownership is not legally separate. Avoid treating sales receipts as money freely available for household use: stock replacement, unpaid bills and other obligations must be considered.

A feasibility check asks whether the enterprise can obtain customers, resources and enough income to cover its costs. List start-up assets separately from recurring expenses and stock. Confirm access to workspace, equipment, inputs and suitable skills. Check applicable requirements with reliable local authorities before opening; requirements differ by location and activity, so a textbook should not invent a universal permit rule.

A first-month plan should state the target customer, offer, starting quantity, price, spending limit and daily records. Assign dates to purchasing, production and customer testing. Set review criteria before launch, such as repeat purchases, delivery reliability and adequate cash for restocking. If results are weak, identify whether demand, price, quality or costs need adjustment rather than borrowing automatically to continue an untested idea.
examples: Teaching start-up table: equipment 60,000; opening stock 40,000; packaging 10,000; reserve cash 20,000. Total required = 130,000 currency units. Equipment is a longer-use asset; opening stock is intended for sale; reserve remains cash until used.

An owner receives 50,000 in sales but owes 25,000 for stock and 10,000 for transport. Only looking at the cash received exaggerates available resources. Record obligations before deciding whether a withdrawal is affordable.

A one-week trial sells 16 of 20 planned items and delivers 14 on time. Sales completion = 16/20 = 80%; on-time rate among actual orders = 14/16 = 87.5%. Different denominators answer different questions.

chapters.title: Financing decisions, microfinance and cooperative organisation
objectives: Compare sources of capital using cost, timing and obligations.
Explain how microfinance and cooperatives support enterprise.
Assess a finance proposal without recommending a provider.
paragraphs: Capital for a small business may come from savings, loans, family or friends, and deferred payment to suppliers. Savings avoid contractual interest but reduce the owner’s reserve for other needs. A loan creates repayment obligations even when sales disappoint. Family funds may be a gift, loan or ownership contribution; clarify which arrangement is intended so expectations about repayment and decision-making are explicit.

Deferred payment allows goods to be obtained now and paid for later. It can help match payments with sales, but goods may cost more than under cash terms and a late payment can damage supplier trust. Compare the full amount payable, payment dates, penalties or fees if any, and the realistic cash available at those dates. A low advertised instalment does not establish the lowest total cost.

Microfinance refers broadly to relatively small-scale financial services for people or enterprises that may have limited access to conventional finance. Depending on the organisation, services can include savings, small loans or financial education. Group arrangements may use peer support or shared responsibility, which can create pressure as well as assistance. Read the actual terms and ask how missed payments affect the individual and group; no provider or product is automatically suitable.

A cooperative is an organisation formed by members to meet shared economic or social needs through joint activity and member participation. Members may pool savings, purchase inputs or market produce together. Joint action can improve bargaining power and spread service costs, but weak records, poor participation or misuse of funds can harm members. Sound operation requires transparent accounts, agreed rules, elected accountability and informed decisions; the exact legal structure and obligations must be verified locally.
examples: Compare two hypothetical funding offers: A provides 100,000 with total scheduled repayment 112,000; B provides 100,000 with repayment 108,000 plus a compulsory non-refundable fee of 6,000. Total stated cost is A 12,000 and B 14,000. This comparison excludes unstated charges and does not evaluate timing or suitability.
A supplier charges 40,000 cash or 44,000 after one month for the same goods. Deferred payment adds 4,000, equal to 10% of the cash price for that period. This is not an annual rate calculation.

Ten cooperative members each contribute 8,000 to a shared input purchase. Pool = 80,000. If inputs cost 72,000 and transport 5,000, the balance is 3,000. Record contributions, invoices and the agreed treatment of the remaining balance.

chapters.title: Managing cash, budgets, profit and corrective action
objectives: Distinguish profit from cash availability.
Prepare and interpret a cash budget.
Use records and management functions to correct problems.
paragraphs: Management coordinates people and resources to achieve business objectives. Planning decides targets and actions; organising assigns work and resources; leading communicates and supports action; control compares actual results with plans and makes corrections. These functions interact: a missed delivery can reveal an unrealistic plan, unclear responsibility or a resource shortage. Blaming a worker without checking the system may leave the cause unresolved.

Records provide evidence for decisions. Keep dated source documents such as receipts and invoices, then record cash received, cash paid, sales, purchases, inventory and amounts owed where relevant. Credit sales create revenue and a customer debt but no immediate cash receipt. Buying equipment uses cash, yet its full cost is not necessarily treated as one period’s operating expense in a developed accounting system. State the simplifying assumptions used in classroom calculations.

For a simple trading period, gross profit equals sales revenue minus cost of goods sold. Operating profit in a simplified exercise subtracts other operating expenses. Cost of goods sold equals opening inventory plus purchases minus closing inventory, assuming the figures cover comparable goods and no other adjustments. Unsold stock is not automatically all charged as goods sold. Personal withdrawals are not an operating expense, although they reduce cash.

A cash budget estimates opening cash, expected receipts and expected payments for each period. Closing cash equals opening cash plus receipts minus payments. A profitable enterprise can face a cash shortage when customers pay late or money is tied up in inventory. Compare actual and budgeted figures, investigate the reason for variances, and take proportionate action such as improving collection, revising purchase timing or addressing waste. Cutting essential quality or safety to meet a budget can create larger losses.
examples: Opening inventory 20,000 + purchases 70,000 − closing inventory 15,000 gives cost of goods sold 75,000. Sales 110,000 − 75,000 = gross profit 35,000. Other operating expenses 18,000 give simplified operating profit 17,000.

Cash budget table: opening cash 12,000; receipts 40,000; supplier payments 28,000; transport 6,000; owner withdrawal 5,000. Closing cash = 12,000 + 40,000 − 28,000 − 6,000 − 5,000 = 13,000. The withdrawal affects cash but is not an operating expense.

Budgeted material cost is 30,000 and actual cost 36,000. Variance is 6,000 over budget. Investigate price changes, extra output and wastage before concluding poor performance; extra output may explain part of the difference.

chapters.title: Warehousing, stock control and a practical enterprise project
objectives: Explain warehouse functions and inventory records.
Calculate stock balances and reorder needs.
Test a local enterprise using operational evidence.
paragraphs: Warehousing is the organised storage and handling of goods until they are needed. It helps bridge time between production and consumption, protects stock and supports reliable supply. A warehouse may be a simple secure storeroom rather than a large specialised building. Suitable storage depends on the product: moisture, heat, pests, theft and contamination create different risks. Follow verified product-specific storage instructions where required.

Inventory includes goods for sale, raw materials and partly completed products where relevant. Stock control records receipts, issues and balances so the business knows what should be available. A stock card records one item consistently by unit, with date, reference, quantities received, quantities issued and balance. Physical counts test whether records match reality; differences can arise from errors, damage, spoilage or theft and should be investigated rather than silently altered.

Stock rotation reduces avoidable loss. First-in, first-out issues older receipts before newer ones; first-expiry, first-out prioritises goods with the earliest expiry date. The two methods can give different orders when a later delivery expires sooner. Keep aisles clear, stack safely, separate incompatible goods and mark damaged stock for assessment. A high stock balance is not always beneficial because it ties up cash and may increase deterioration.

A reorder decision considers average demand during supplier lead time plus a safety buffer. The calculation is only a planning aid: demand and delivery times can change. Apply these ideas in a small enterprise project by identifying a local need, surveying customers, budgeting a limited trial, recording stock and sales, and reviewing profit, cash and customer feedback. Use locally observed evidence rather than assuming an opportunity exists simply because a product is common elsewhere.
examples: Stock-card table for exercise books: opening 50; receive 30 → balance 80; issue 45 → 35; receive 20 → 55; damaged 3 removed after authorisation → 52. Record damage separately from sales so revenue is not overstated.
Average demand is 8 units/day, lead time 4 days and safety stock 10 units. Simplified reorder point = 8 × 4 + 10 = 42 units. Review the assumptions if demand or lead time changes.

Batch A arrived first but expires in August; Batch B arrived later but expires in June. FIFO would issue A first by arrival; FEFO issues B first because June expiry is earlier. Inspect actual product condition as well as dates.
